---
title: Compatibility
description: Start an Atlas theme from a shadcn or tweakcn theme.
icon: Puzzle
---

Atlas's base tokens are the shadcn/ui token set, verbatim. The names, and what each one means, are unchanged.

So a shadcn theme, or anything generated by a tool that targets shadcn such as tweakcn, is already most of an Atlas theme. The work is mechanical.

<Callout type="info">
  Atlas will do this conversion for you. Settings → Appearance → **Import** takes a shadcn registry item or a pasted `globals.css` and writes the theme file, along with a report of what it kept and what it had to invent. See [importing a theme](/docs/themes/importing). This page is the same conversion by hand, and explains what the format can and cannot say.
</Callout>

## Convert the tokens

A shadcn theme is CSS custom properties in a `:root` block and a `.dark` block. Atlas wants the same names without the leading `--`, as TOML keys under `[light.base]` and `[dark.base]`.

```css title="shadcn"
.dark {
  --background: #08070a;
  --foreground: #e0def4;
  --card: #18151e;
  --primary: #eb6f92;
  --radius: 8px;
}
```

```toml title="Atlas"
[dark.base]
background = "#08070a"
foreground = "#e0def4"
card = "#18151e"
primary = "#eb6f92"
radius = "8px"
```

In shadcn, `:root` is the light theme and `.dark` is the dark one, so they become `[light.base]` and `[dark.base]` respectively. Carry both across if your source has both: Atlas's Light and System modes are on, and a theme with one variant is used for the other as well.

Atlas accepts `oklch()` as well as hex, `rgb()`, and `hsl()`, so a tweakcn export usually pastes straight across.

<Callout type="warn">
  Older shadcn themes write bare HSL channels, as in `--background: 0 0% 100%`. Atlas needs a complete colour, so wrap those: `background = "hsl(0 0% 100%)"`.
</Callout>

## Fill in the rest of the required set

All 45 base tokens must be present in each variant you ship. A shadcn theme normally covers the colours, `radius`, the charts, and the sidebar family. It often does not cover the rest.

Copy these from any built-in Atlas theme if your source has no opinion, giving a light variant a lighter shadow ramp than the dark values below:

```toml
font-sans = "-apple-system, \"SF Pro Text\", system-ui, sans-serif"
font-serif = "ui-serif, Georgia, Cambria, \"Times New Roman\", serif"
font-mono = "\"SF Mono\", \"Geist Mono\", \"JetBrains Mono\", monospace"
tracking-normal = "0em"
spacing = "0.25rem"
shadow-2xs = "0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35)"
shadow-xs = "0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.45)"
shadow-sm = "0 1px 3px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.55)"
shadow-md = "0 4px 12px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65)"
shadow-lg = "0 8px 24px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.75)"
shadow-xl = "0 12px 36px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.82)"
shadow-2xl = "0 16px 48px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)"
```

Drop anything your source emits that is not one of the 45. Atlas rejects a base token it does not recognise, and a generator's extra variables are the usual reason a converted file will not load.

## What the conversion gives you

Everything the base tokens reach, which is most of the window: the app background, panels, the rail, tabs, cards and popovers, borders, the focus ring, the signature colour, the editor background and default text, selections, charts, the radius scale, the fonts, and the elevation.

That is a complete, working theme. It will load and it will look like your palette.

Two shadcn tokens carry more weight in Atlas than they do in a web app, so give them a second look. `chart-1` through `chart-5` are five series that have to stay tellable apart, since two that differ only slightly render as one line. And `ring` is a real accent, used for the focus ring and the matching-bracket outline, so a `ring` set to a grey leaves the editor without one.

## What a shadcn theme cannot say

A shadcn token set describes an interface. Atlas keeps its names exactly, so the 45 you converted sit inside the larger set Atlas colours from, and everything outside them is worked out rather than asked for.

<Mermaid chart={`
flowchart LR
    subgraph A["what Atlas colours"]
        direction LR
        B["the 45 you converted<br/>chrome, panels, editor<br/>background, charts"]
        R["syntax, terminal, diff,<br/>status, search<br/>derived, not written"]
        B ~~~ R
    end
`} />

It has no vocabulary for the things a code tool needs:

- **Syntax highlighting.** No keyword, string, type, or comment colour.
- **Terminal ANSI colours.** No red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, or cyan.
- **Diff tints.** No addition or removal colour.
- **Status hues.** No success, warning, or informational colour beyond `destructive`.
- **Search highlights.** No match colour.

Atlas will derive all of them rather than leave them unstyled, but with nothing to derive from it falls back to its own defaults, and those will not match your theme.

**Add a palette.** Eight lines fix all five groups at once:

```toml
[dark.palette]
red = "#eb6f92"
orange = "#ebbcba"
yellow = "#f6c177"
green = "#31748f"
cyan = "#9ccfd8"
blue = "#9ccfd8"
purple = "#c4a7e7"
pink = "#ebbcba"
```

This is the single step that turns a converted interface theme into an Atlas theme. The names are hues rather than slots, and everything downstream trusts them, so file each colour under the name it actually is.

See the [token reference](/docs/themes/tokens) for what each hue feeds. After the palette, the keys worth adding by hand are the fifteen syntax roles and the ten editor keys. No built-in theme sets a terminal, status, search, or agent key at all, because a good palette already gets those right.

## What Atlas does with the extras

Three tokens come along with a shadcn or tweakcn theme and behave differently from the rest:

- **`spacing`.** Atlas's density is designed around Tailwind's default `0.25rem`, and every built-in theme uses it. Keep that value unless a different density is what you are after.
- **`tracking-normal`.** Required by the set, and Atlas does not currently read it.
- **The shadow ramp.** Atlas renders three elevations: `shadow-sm` raised, `shadow-2xl` for menus and popovers, and `shadow-xl` stacked beneath `shadow-2xl` for dialogs. The other four shadow tokens are required but unused, so do not spend time tuning them.
